title: The master and the leg
hookLine: enslaved, Epictetus warns his master he'll break his leg, it breaks, and he says calmly "didn't I tell you?"
last: MARCUS AURELIUS — UP, TO DO A HUMAN'S WORK.

cards: Picture this. A wealthy man in Rome, so the story goes, starts twisting the leg of Epictetus, the man he owns. Hard.
For no reason we're told. And Epictetus, instead of crying out, looks at his master and speaks, quietly: you're going to break it.

teach.b: He was born enslaved, at the very bottom of the empire, in a town in what's now Turkey. Epictetus, the only name we have for him, is a Greek word for acquired. Bought.
His owner was himself a former slave of the emperor Nero's household. The master keeps twisting. The leg breaks.
And Epictetus says, calmly: didn't I tell you it would break? No scream, no curse. Now, honesty about the source.

teach.h: A STORY TOLD BY A CRITIC.
teach.b: This story isn't from Epictetus. It comes from an ancient writer named Celsus, in a book attacking Christianity, and we only have it because a Christian scholar, Origen, quoted Celsus in order to answer him.
Another ancient source says his lameness came from illness, not cruelty. So we can't be sure it happened. But we know Epictetus was lame, and we know what he taught about it.

teach.h: IMPEDIMENT TO THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.
teach.b: In George Long's translation of his handbook: "Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will." And the handbook's first line: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not."
A twisted leg isn't in your power, if someone stronger is doing the twisting.

What you say while it happens may still be yours. What this doesn't mean: that cruelty is fine, or that pain doesn't hurt, or that someone being harmed should just keep quiet. If it happened, it was wrong.

The story is about something smaller and stranger: even at the very bottom, with no power at all, a person can still choose the voice they answer in. Epictetus spent the rest of his life teaching that.

how: Stoic practice sorts troubles into what is in our power and what is not, and puts effort only into the first: our own judgments, choices and responses.

o: a Greek doctor who wrote an early book on healing
an enslaved man in Rome who became a Stoic teacher
a Roman senator who spoke out against the emperor Nero

games.q: the story and its sources — tap the pairs.
p: says the lameness came from illness

s: the leg story comes from Epictetus's own writings
it comes from Celsus, preserved because Origen quoted him.
and he taught that lameness is an impediment to the leg, not the will.
the story means cruelty is fine if you stay calm
the leg was broken, and it was wrong. the story is about the voice you answer in.

games.q: you're Epictetus. your master is twisting your leg, hard. what do you say?
o: "you're going to break it." and when it breaks: "didn't I tell you?"
games.why: in the story he warns him, and when the leg breaks, says calmly, "didn't I tell you it would break?"

practice: Sit, and let the breath settle, then gently notice one pain you can't change today: a sore back, a diagnosis, a person who won't change, a loss.
Don't push it away and don't feed it; breathe beside it, and ask quietly what part of it is yours, maybe only the voice you answer in. If it's too much today, just come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Epictetus. An enslaved man, a broken leg, and a calm answer: didn't I tell you?

orig.note: Greek: acquired, gained. The name of an enslaved man who became a teacher of philosophy.

carryVoice: Your line: said calmly. Even with no power at all, the voice you answer in can stay yours. That's day twenty-three.
